body: Intro · resources · crops & horticulture
Grade 11 is the *foundation* year before Grade 12 livestock/forest/soil-water/management. Three units. Flip cards and a quiz after each unit.

units.title: Introduction to Agriculture
units.intro: Agriculture is the science and art of growing plants and raising animals for food, fibre, fuel and income. It is how societies eat — and in Eritrea it is still the main livelihood.

cards.title: What agriculture means
body: The word **agriculture** comes from two Latin words: **ager** = soil or land, and **cultura** = cultivation (tilling the land). So the word itself means "looking after the land to grow things".

**Definition (learn it):** agriculture is the organized production of **food, feed** (for animals) and **fibres**. A broader definition adds the **processing and marketing** of crops, livestock and their by-products.
Agriculture is both a **science** and an **art**:
- **Science** — it uses scientific methods and knowledge (soil chemistry, plant breeding, animal nutrition).
- **Art** — it also needs skill and judgement that only practice gives (when to plough, how deep, which ox to pair with which).
**Eritrean example:** a farmer near Mendefera decides to sow barley after the first good rain in June (art: reading the season) and uses an improved seed from the Ministry of Agriculture (science).

cards.title: The story of agriculture in five stages
body: Read the figure from top to bottom: each stage kept what was useful from the stage before.

cards.title: 1.1.1 From hunting and gathering to crop and livestock production
body: Nobody knows exactly where and when agriculture began, because people in many places started to grow crops and keep animals. What we do know is the order of the steps:

**Step 1 — Hunting, fishing and gathering.** Early people hunted animals, fished, and gathered fruits, leaves, bark and honey. They moved often, owned almost no private property and stored very little.

**Step 2 — Settling and planting.** Life slowly became more settled. People planted some crops to add to wild food and began to **store surplus** for lean times. Storage is the first big advantage of farming.

**Step 3 — Domestication of animals.** The **dog** is believed to be the first domesticated animal (hunting, guarding, company). The **goat** probably came next, to secure food when hunting was poor. The **horse** was among the first animals tamed for draught and carrying loads.
**Step 4 — Better methods.** People selected better seed (sound propagating material such as seeds, bulbs and tubers), better breeds, built irrigation to add to rainfall, improved tools and storage.
**Step 5 — Mechanisation and information.** Tractors, harvesters and combines now plough, plant and harvest far faster, with less labour and time, while keeping product quality.
**In Eritrea** farming is believed to have started about **4000 years ago**. Most people still grow crops, keep animals, or do both.

cards.title: Why domesticated animals spread so widely
body: Domesticated animals **thrive under artificial conditions** and **reproduce regularly in confinement**; wild animals rarely do. That is why herders could carry them to new places.

As they spread, animals **adapted** to new environments. Example: the humped **zebu cattle** of Eritrea (Arado in the highlands, Barka in the western lowlands) tolerate heat, ticks and poor grazing much better than European breeds; the European **Holstein-Friesian** gives far more milk but needs cool weather and good feed.

cards.title: Remember
body: **ager** + **cultura** = agriculture.
Order: hunting/gathering → settling + storing → domestication (dog first, then goat) → improved seed, breeds, irrigation → mechanisation.
Farming in Eritrea: about **4000 years** old.

cards.title: Worked example — the advantage of settling
cards.problem: Exercise 1.1 Q2: What advantages did settling in one place and growing crops and animals give early humans compared with hunting and gathering?

steps.text: Think of what was **uncertain** in hunting: food might not be found. Farming makes food **more available and predictable**.
Think of **ownership**: the crop or the herd belongs to the family that raised it.
Think of **time**: a surplus can be **stored** for the dry season or a drought.
Think of **choice**: people grow the foods they **prefer** (e.g. barley, teff) instead of eating whatever is found.

cards.answer: More reliable food, ownership of the product, stored surplus for lean times, and preferred foods.

cards.title: Worked example — components of modern agriculture
cards.problem: Exercise 1.1 Q3: List some components of modern agriculture.

steps.text: Start from the **inputs**: improved seed and breeds, fertilizers, pesticides, veterinary drugs.
Add **water**: irrigation systems that supplement rainfall (e.g. drip irrigation at Sawa-Afhimbol).
Add **machines**: tractors, planters, harvesters and combines.
Add **knowledge**: agricultural information, research and extension, good storage methods.

cards.answer: Improved seed and breeds, fertilizer and pesticides, irrigation, mechanisation, good storage, and information/extension.

cards.title: Ten roles of agriculture
body: An exam may ask for "five roles". Pick any five and give **one Eritrean example** for each.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Food supply
body: Agriculture feeds the nation. Eritrean farms produce:
- **Cereals:** wheat, barley, sorghum, pearl millet, finger millet and teff (taff).
- **Pulses:** peas, beans, lentils (and chickpea, faba bean).
- **Oil crops:** sesame, groundnut, Niger seed, linseed, cottonseed.
- **Fruits:** bananas, oranges, lemons, mangos, guavas, apples.
- **Vegetables:** cabbage, kale, onion, tomato, lettuce.
- **Animal foods:** meat, milk, eggs, honey, and by-products such as cream, butter, cheese and yogurt.
Together these give the **carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals** people need. Example: injera from teff or sorghum (carbohydrate) eaten with shiro from chickpea or peas (protein).

cards.title: 1.2.2 Source of income
body: Farmers earn money by selling fruits, vegetables, grain, oil seeds, cotton, **live animals** (cattle, sheep, goats, poultry) and **animal products** (hides and skins, milk, butter, honey) on local markets or for export.
As agriculture grows it also creates income for **other businesses**: factories that make animal feed, herbicides, pesticides and veterinary drugs, and traders and transporters.
**Example:** a family near Keren sells goats at the Monday livestock market to pay school fees.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Earner of foreign currency
body: Exported farm products bring **foreign currency**: live animals, skins and hides, meat, milk products, oil seeds (especially sesame), cotton, fresh or processed fruit and vegetables, flowers, spices, gums and resins.
Eritrea uses this currency to **import** what it does not produce: petroleum, farm machinery, electronic equipment, medicine and fertilizer.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Raw materials for industry
body: Agro-industries depend on farm products:
- **Edible oil** from sesame, cottonseed and Niger seed.
- **Flour and pasta** from wheat and other grains.
- **Beer** from malting barley.
- **Sugar** from sugar cane and sugar beet.
- **Textiles** from cotton and wool.
- **Dairy products** (cheese, butter, yogurt, powdered milk) from milk; **canned meat** from meat.
- **Shoes, bags and belts** from hides and skins (leather industry).
Processing gives useful **by-products** too: **oil-seed cake** and **molasses** are good animal feeds — another link between crops and livestock.

cards.title: 1.2.5 Employment
body: Agriculture is the main source of livelihood in rural Eritrea: about **70 per cent** of the population is agrarian (p. 17).

Besides the farm family, dairy, poultry and horticultural farms, processing plants, input shops, markets and transport all **employ people**. A strong farm sector keeps young people in the villages instead of moving to towns without work.

cards.title: 1.2.6 Source of fuel
body: Most rural kitchens burn **wood, charcoal and dung**, all from agriculture and forests.
**Watch out:** burning dung and crop residues for fuel takes organic matter and nutrients away from the soil. That is why improved stoves (such as the Eritrean **Adhanet** mogogo) are encouraged.

cards.title: 1.2.7 Socio-cultural heritage
body: Livestock have social value: they act as **insurance or a bank** for rural families (sell an ox in a bad year), and they bring **prestige** — in Eritrea a farmer with many animals commands more respect. Animals are also given at weddings and slaughtered at holidays.

cards.title: 1.2.8 Environmental impact (positive and negative)
body: Agriculture can harm or help the environment.

cards.title: Environmental impact of agriculture
head: Negative effects
Positive effects
rows: Soil contamination from misuse of pesticides and fertilizers
Air pollution from chemicals and burning

cards.title: 1.2.9 Source of energy (draught power)
body: Oxen, camels, donkeys and horses supply **energy** for ploughing, transport and carrying water. Two oxen pulling a **maresha** (traditional plough) save many days of hoeing; a donkey carries water and grain to and from the market.

cards.title: 1.2.10 Source of construction materials
body: Wood for houses, furniture and fence poles comes from planted or natural trees. **Straw of sorghum and pearl millet** is used for fencing, walls and roofing — for example the round huts (agudo) of the western lowlands.

cards.title: Worked example — products and by-products
cards.problem: Exercise 1.2 Q3: Name industries that get raw materials from agriculture, with their products and by-products.

steps.text: Write each industry with its raw material and product: oil mill (sesame, Niger seed) → edible oil.
Add the by-product: **oil-seed cake** → animal feed.
Sugar factory (sugar cane) → sugar; by-product **molasses** → animal feed.
Flour mill (wheat) → flour, pasta; by-product **bran** → feed. Brewery (malting barley) → beer; spent grain → feed.
Dairy (milk) → butter, cheese, yogurt; tannery (hides, skins) → leather, shoes, bags; textile mill (cotton, wool) → cloth.

cards.answer: Oil mill → oil + cake; sugar → sugar + molasses; flour mill → flour + bran; brewery → beer; dairy → butter, cheese; tannery → leather; textile → cloth.

cards.title: Memory trick — the ten roles in textbook order
body: Food, Income, Foreign currency, Raw materials, Employment, Fuel, Socio-cultural, Environment, Energy (draught), Construction. Say them in the order of the textbook sections 1.2.1 to 1.2.10.

cards.title: Roles of agriculture
body: Food security, raw materials (cotton, hides), jobs, export earnings, rural life, manure that returns to the field. Weak agriculture → people leave the land and cities swell.

cards.title: 1.3 What a farming system is
body: **A farming system** is the way the parts of a farm (land, crops, animals, family labour, tools, money) are **linked together**. The links include draught power, feed, manure, capital and social ties.
Eritrean agriculture has stayed at **subsistence** level for generations: smallholders and agro-pastoralists manage about **95 %** of the cultivated land.
- **Subsistence farmers** have few resources and eat most of what they produce, with little left to sell.
- **Commercial farmers** produce mainly to **sell** and earn income, using more inputs and modern technology.
Eritrea has **three major farming systems** — nomadic pastoralism, semi-nomadic pastoralism and sedentary agro-pastoralism — plus **intensive commercial** systems.

cards.title: How many people follow each system
a) Nomadic pastoralism
body: **Pastoralism** = a farming system where **animals are the main component**. **Nomadism** = not settling in one place.
- **Where:** dry, thinly populated semi-desert areas (0.8–10 people per km²): the **Red Sea coastal areas** and the **north-western lowlands**.
- **How:** the **whole family moves** with the herd in search of pasture and water.
- **Animals:** cattle are the most important (kept mainly for **milk**, not meat), with camels, sheep, goats and donkeys. Rainfall, water and disease decide the mix.
- **Land:** owned and grazed **communally**. Wealth and prestige are counted in animals, not money.
- **Value:** the source of most male animals sold in urban markets.
- **Problem:** schools, clinics and veterinary services are hard to deliver to people who keep moving. Nomadism is now giving way to settled agro-pastoralism.

cards.title: b) Semi-nomadic pastoralism and transhumance
body: Semi-nomadic pastoralists have a **village base** and stay for some months where water and pasture are good; they then move with the animals to **seasonal grazing areas**, where they may also plant crops (sometimes in riverbeds).

**Transhumance** is one form: the seasonal movement of people and livestock between zones — for example from the **hot lowlands to the cool highlands** during the hot season, and back when the lowland rains come.
It is easier to bring basic services to semi-nomadic communities than to nomads. In Eritrea it occurs in **spate irrigation** areas such as **Sheeb** (Northern Red Sea).

cards.title: c) Sedentary agro-pastoralism (mixed farming)
body: Families live in **permanent villages**, grow crops and keep livestock. This is **mixed farming**, the system of the **moist and arid highlands** (e.g. around Asmara, Mendefera, Adi Keyh). It can be intensive or extensive, for cash or for subsistence.
Systems in Eritrea that integrate crops and livestock:
- rain-fed **cereal–pulse** production
- the crop–livestock mixed system
- the agro-pastoralist rain-fed system
- small-scale **irrigated horticulture**
- agro-pastoral **spate irrigation**

cards.title: The two-way link in mixed farming
body: Crops give straw, stover and bran to the animals; animals give manure (fertility) and draught power (oxen pull the maresha) back to the crops.

cards.title: d) Intensive commercial systems
body: **Intensive** = high inputs per hectare and per animal to get high output. Three examples:

**i) Peri-urban dairy** — around Asmara, Keren and other towns, to sell milk. Breed: **Holstein-Friesian** and its crosses with local cattle. A Holstein can give **35–40 litres a day** in countries with well-developed dairies, but much less in Eritrea because of constraints. Feeds: crop residues, hay, alfalfa, elephant grass, wheat bran, wheat middlings, sorghum husk and sesame cake. Constraints: feed shortage, little land for forage and housing, poor husbandry, weak extension and veterinary services, diseases (tuberculosis, brucellosis, foot-and-mouth disease, mastitis).

**ii) Commercial poultry** — most eggs still come from free-ranging village chickens, but commercial farms keep the **White Leghorn** in houses with feeders and drinkers. It suits warm climates and lays **up to 270 eggs a year**. Common diseases: Newcastle disease, Gumboro, Marek's disease, respiratory diseases.

**iii) Commercial farms** — profit-oriented, selling to local or foreign markets. State farms such as **Elabered**, **Sawa-Afhimbol Agro-Industries** (drip irrigation) and **Alighidir** (cotton), plus fast-growing private farms producing cereals, oil seeds, fruit, vegetables and livestock.

cards.title: Worked example — nomadic vs semi-nomadic
cards.problem: Exercise 1.3 Q1: Explain the differences between nomadic and semi-nomadic pastoralism.

steps.text: Compare **who moves**: nomads move with the whole family all year; semi-nomads keep a village base and move the herd seasonally.
Compare **crops**: nomads grow none; semi-nomads may plant crops in riverbeds or at seasonal grazing areas.
Compare **services**: easier to provide schools and clinics to semi-nomads.
Give the **share and place**: nomadic 11 % (coast, north-west); semi-nomadic 22 % (e.g. Sheeb spate area).

cards.answer: Nomads move the whole family all year and do not farm; semi-nomads have a base village, move seasonally and may grow some crops.

cards.title: Why Eritrea does not yet grow enough food
body: More than **70 %** of Eritreans are farmers, yet the country still does not produce enough food. A **constraint** is anything that holds production back. The textbook sorts constraints in **two ways** — learn both.

cards.title: Way 1 — by effect on yield (Table 1.3)
head: Group
Meaning
Examples
rows: Given conditions; production cannot happen without them; beyond the farmer's control
CO₂ concentration, solar radiation, temperature, humidity, altitude and latitude, crop physiology, species, breeds, varieties

cards.title: Quick test for the three groups
body: Ask: **Can the farmer change it?** No → defining (altitude, sunlight). **Can he add it?** → limiting (water, fertilizer, feed). **Does he have to fight it?** → reducing (pests, weeds, disease).

cards.title: 1.4.1 Natural factors
body: **a) Biotic factors** — caused by living things; they lower both **quality and quantity**.
- Insects: locusts and grasshoppers, armyworms, stalk-borers, weevils.
- Diseases of crops and livestock caused by bacteria, fungi and viruses.
- Livestock parasites: external (ticks, fleas, lice, mites) and internal (gastro-intestinal and blood parasites).
- Weeds compete with the crop for **water, light and nutrients**. Parasitic weed: **Striga** (witchweed) on sorghum roots. Other weeds: wild oats in barley and wheat.

**b) Abiotic factors** — from non-living things. Rainfall in most of Eritrea is **low, unevenly distributed and falls in heavy showers** over a short time. It often starts early and stops before the crop has finished filling grain, so repeated **droughts** cut yields.

**c) Climate change** — greenhouse gases (**CO₂, CH₄, CFCs, N₂O**) trap heat. Results: higher temperatures, less and more erratic rain. Burning dung and crop residues for fuel, deforestation, grass burning and erosion all reduce the soil's ability to store carbon.

cards.title: 1.4.2 Anthropogenic (human-made) factors
body: **a) Land degradation** — the land's physical, biological and economic potential declines. Causes: **overgrazing, over-cultivation, deforestation**, made worse by drought, steep slopes and torrential rain. Human history adds to it: trees cut for trenches and villages burned during the independence war, and land confiscation and tree destruction under Italian colonial rule. Effects: lower yields per input, fewer livestock, loss of vegetation, fuel-wood shortage, loss of topsoil.

**b) Land tenure** — the system of owning, leasing or using land. Traditional systems: **dessa** (village land, redistributed; common in the highlands; average holding about **1 ha**; women had no land rights), **risti** (kinship land) and **demaniale** (state land). **Land Law No. 58 of 1994** made the state the owner and gave every Eritrean, **including women**, the right of **usufruct** (use). Redistribution every **5–7 years** still discourages long-term investment such as terraces; communal rangeland encourages overgrazing.

**c) Soil erosion** — the removal of topsoil by **water or wind**. Organic matter is already low, so soils hold less water and crops suffer in dry spells. Estimated losses: **50–100 t/ha/year** in the highlands, **47** in the moist lowlands, **37** on the eastern escarpment and about **6** in the dry lowlands.

**d) Inappropriate land use** — ploughing steep slopes and building houses on fertile plains. Traditionally hills were for settlement and grazing and plains for crops; urban growth is breaking this rule. **Land-use planning** allocates land to farming, settlement, forest, grazing and roads according to carrying capacity.

cards.title: 1.4.3 Socio-economic factors
body: - **Poor marketing and storage:** little credit, little price information, shortages of fertilizer, seed, pesticides, drugs and spare parts; perishable produce is lost on the way to market without cold rooms, silos or warehouses.
- **Inadequate inputs:** too little fertilizer, improved seed, chemicals, better breeds and machinery. Local seed is well adapted but low-yielding.
- **Poor infrastructure:** mountains and plains make it hard to link farms to markets and factories, although many roads, bridges and dams have been built since independence.
- **Lack of know-how:** many farmers cannot read, extension is thin, and tradition is hard to change (e.g. herders keep large herds instead of investing their value).
- **Effects of war:** bombing and fires destroyed crops, livestock and trees; the 1998–2000 border war hit the sector hard.
- **Inadequate technical inputs:** primitive tools and a low-input, low-output system.

cards.title: Worked example — classifying constraints
cards.problem: Classify each by effect on yield: (a) altitude of Asmara (2 325 m); (b) a nitrogen shortage in a teff field; (c) Striga in a sorghum field; (d) the Arado breed of a cow.

steps.text: (a) Altitude cannot be changed by the farmer → **yield-defining**.
(b) Nitrogen can be supplied as fertilizer or manure → **yield-limiting**.
(c) Striga is a weed that takes away yield → **yield-reducing**.
(d) The breed sets the genetic ceiling of milk yield → **yield-defining**.

cards.title: Worked example — soil loss on a farm
cards.problem: A farmer has 2 ha on the eastern escarpment and 3 ha in the dry lowlands. Using the textbook estimates, how much soil is lost each year?

steps.text: Escarpment: 2 ha × 37 t/ha = **74 t**.
Dry lowlands: 3 ha × 6 t/ha = **18 t**.
Total: 74 + 18 = **92 t** every year — about 9 large truckloads.

cards.q: Which of the following soil nutrients is a primary macronutrient, needed in large amounts and commonly supplied as urea?

cards.title: Agriculture is an applied, multidisciplinary science
body: Agricultural science rests on **basic sciences**: biology, chemistry, physics, mathematics, geography and economics.
- **Mathematics:** animal and plant breeding, soil physics, agricultural economics.
- **Chemistry:** animal nutrition, soil fertility, plant protection, food processing, fertilizer formulation.
- **Physics:** soil physics, densities, nutrient and water transport.
- **Botany** (plant classification), **zoology** (animal science, entomology, microbiology) and **genetics** (the foundation of breeding).
For convenience the subject is split into **three groups**: plant sciences, animal sciences, and production support and management systems.

cards.title: 1.5.1 Plant sciences
body: - **Horticulture:** fruits, vegetables, flowers, ornamentals, spices, medicinal and aromatic plants; also environmental horticulture (home gardens, landscaping, parks) and horticultural therapy.

- **Agronomy** (Greek *agros* = field, *nomos* = to manage): principles and practice of **field-crop** production — cereals, pulses, oil, industrial and forage crops — including breeding and management.
- **Soil science:** soil formation, classification, mapping, physical, chemical and biological properties.
- **Forestry:** the art and science of managing forests, plantations and related resources.
- **Forage and pasture:** producing forage plants and managing pastures for animals.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Animal sciences
body: - **Animal husbandry:** keeping cattle, sheep, goats, camels, equines, poultry, pigs, rabbits and bees — breeding, feeding and management.
- **Animal nutrition:** feeding a balanced diet for optimum production.
- **Animal breeding:** improving animals by **selection** within a breed or **crossing** with other breeds (e.g. Holstein × Arado crosses).
- **Rangeland management:** maintaining and improving grazing land.
- **Aquaculture:** farming fish, shrimps, crabs, lobsters and oysters in ponds under controlled feeding and management.

cards.title: 1.5.3 Production support and management systems
body: - **Irrigation and drainage engineering:** irrigation brings water from a source to the crop through canals or pipes (spate, sprinkler, basin, furrow, drip); **drainage** removes excess water from the surface and upper subsoil.
- **Soil and water conservation engineering:** terraces, check dams, bunds — reducing soil loss and protecting water supply.
- **Agricultural economics:** choosing the best combination of limited resources to **maximise profit**.
- **Agricultural extension:** educating farmers so they apply new knowledge.
- **Agricultural mechanisation:** machines for production, processing and transport — saves labour and time.
- **Post-harvest and food-processing engineering:** cutting losses in quality and quantity.
- **Plant protection:** keeping plants healthy and controlling insects, rodents, birds and weeds by integrated pest management (IPM).
- **Veterinary science:** animal diseases and health, including diseases shared with humans (zoonoses).
- **Agro-climatology:** recording, analysing and forecasting weather and climate for farming.
- **Land reclamation:** rehabilitating degraded land and bringing virgin land into farming.

questions.q: In parts of Eritrea, families keep a permanent or semi-permanent village base where they live for several months of the year, often planting crops in riverbeds or under spate irrigation, and during the hot dry season they move with their livestock from the hot lowlands to the cool highlands in search of pasture and water. This seasonal movement, called transhumance, is the defining practice of which farming system described in the unit?
why: **Recall the meaning of transhumance.** Transhumance is the seasonal migration of people and their livestock from the hot lowlands to the cool highlands in search of pasture and water.

**Match the practice to the correct system.** The unit states that semi-nomadic pastoralism is the system in which families establish a permanent or semi-permanent village base, plant crops in riverbeds or under spate irrigation (such as in the Sheeb area), and practise transhumance during the hot dry season. It accounts for approximately $$22\%$$ of the population.

**Check every other option against the unit.** Nomadic pastoralism moves the entire family constantly with no settled base; sedentary agro-pastoralism keeps permanent villages in the highlands without seasonal migration; intensive commercial poultry farms keep birds under confinement for egg production. Each of these contradicts the description, so none is also correct.
**Conclude.** The only system that combines a semi-permanent village base, spate-irrigation cropping and seasonal lowland-to-highland migration is semi-nomadic pastoralism.

why: **List the distinguishing features.** The description gives three key features: communal land ownership, constant movement of the whole family, and livestock kept mainly for milk and social prestige.

**Compare with the unit's systems.** The unit describes nomadic pastoralism as prevalent in the dry, semi-desert zones of the Red Sea coast and the North Western lowlands, with families that do not settle in one place, communal land ownership, and livestock kept primarily for milk and social prestige; it represents about $$11\%$$ of the population.

**Eliminate the other systems.** Semi-nomadic pastoralism has a permanent or semi-permanent village base, sedentary agro-pastoralism has permanent villages with cultivation and livestock on the same farm, and commercial systems are fixed and specialized, so none fits a community that is always on the move.

questions.q: Two $$3\text{-hectare}$$ plots are monitored in Eritrea. Plot A lies on the steep Eastern Escarpment, where the unit estimates annual soil loss at $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$. Plot B lies in the dry lowlands, where annual soil loss is $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$. (a) Calculate the total annual soil loss in tons for each plot. (b) Determine how many times greater the soil loss on Plot A is than on Plot B, and state the difference in tons.
questions.answer: Plot A loses $$111\text{ tons per year}$$ and Plot B loses $$18\text{ tons per year}$$; Plot A loses about $$6.2$$ times as much soil, a difference of $$93\text{ tons per year}$$.
why: **State the working formula.** Total annual soil loss = soil-loss rate per hectare x area of the plot in hectares.
**Compute the loss on Plot A.** Plot A: $$37\text{ tons per hectare} \times 3\text{ ha} = 111\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Compute the loss on Plot B.** Plot B: $$6\text{ tons per hectare} \times 3\text{ ha} = 18\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Find how many times greater Plot A's loss is.** Ratio = $$\dfrac{111}{18} = 6.17$$, which rounds to about $$6.2$$ times.

**Find the difference and conclude.** Difference = $$111 - 18 = 93\text{ tons per year}$$. The Eastern Escarpment plot therefore loses about $$6.2$$ times as much soil as the dry lowland plot, that is, $$93\text{ tons}$$ more each year.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A farmer near Massawa farms two $$5\text{-hectare}$$ plots. The first plot lies in the moist lowlands, where the unit estimates annual soil loss at $$47\text{ tons per hectare}$$; the second lies in the dry lowlands, where the estimate is $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$. Calculate the annual soil loss of each plot and state how many times greater the moist lowland loss is.
questions.answer: The moist lowland plot loses $$235\text{ tons per year}$$ and the dry lowland plot loses $$30\text{ tons per year}$$; the moist lowland loss is about $$7.8$$ times greater.
why: **Apply the soil-loss formula.** Total annual soil loss = rate per hectare x area, so each plot is treated separately with its own unit rate.
**Moist lowland plot.** $$47\text{ tons per hectare} \times 5\text{ ha} = 235\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Dry lowland plot.** $$6\text{ tons per hectare} \times 5\text{ ha} = 30\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Compare the two losses.** Ratio = $$\dfrac{235}{30} = 7.83$$, which rounds to about $$7.8$$ times greater.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: An extension agent compares an $$8\text{-hectare}$$ block of steep highland fields with an $$8\text{-hectare}$$ block on the Eastern Escarpment. The unit gives the minimum steep-highland loss as $$50\text{ tons per hectare}$$ and the Eastern Escarpment loss as $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$. Find the annual soil loss of each block and express the steep-highland excess as a ratio and in tons.
questions.answer: The steep highland block loses $$400\text{ tons per year}$$ and the Eastern Escarpment block loses $$296\text{ tons per year}$$; the steep highland block loses about $$1.35$$ times as much, an excess of $$104\text{ tons per year}$$.
why: **Identify the two unit rates.** Steep highland minimum = $$50\text{ tons per hectare}$$; Eastern Escarpment = $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$; both blocks are $$8\text{ ha}$$.
**Steep highland block.** $$50\text{ tons per hectare} \times 8\text{ ha} = 400\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Eastern Escarpment block.** $$37\text{ tons per hectare} \times 8\text{ ha} = 296\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Ratio and excess.** Ratio = $$\dfrac{400}{296} = 1.35$$; excess = $$400 - 296 = 104\text{ tons per year}$$.

questions.q: A survey of $$2\,000$$ rural households in a district of Eritrea found that their farming systems follow the national pattern given in the unit: $$11\%$$ nomadic pastoralism, $$22\%$$ semi-nomadic pastoralism and $$67\%$$ sedentary agro-pastoralism. Calculate the number of households in the survey that belong to each of the three farming systems, and verify that the three numbers add up to the surveyed total.
questions.answer: $$220$$ nomadic pastoralist, $$440$$ semi-nomadic pastoralist and $$1\,340$$ sedentary agro-pastoralist households; the three figures add up to $$2\,000$$ households.
why: **State the method.** Number of households in a category = percentage of that category x total number of households surveyed, with the percentage written as a decimal fraction.
**Nomadic pastoralist households.** $$0.11 \times 2\,000 = 220$$ households.
**Semi-nomadic pastoralist households.** $$0.22 \times 2\,000 = 440$$ households.
**Sedentary agro-pastoralist households.** $$0.67 \times 2\,000 = 1\,340$$ households.
**Check the total.** $$220 + 440 + 1\,340 = 2\,000$$ households, which equals the number surveyed, so the allocation is consistent.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: In the Anseba region, $$4\,500$$ farming households are classified according to the unit's national pattern of $$11\%$$ nomadic pastoralism, $$22\%$$ semi-nomadic pastoralism and $$67\%$$ sedentary agro-pastoralism. How many households fall into each of the three systems, and how many are not nomadic pastoralists?
questions.answer: $$495$$ nomadic pastoralist, $$990$$ semi-nomadic pastoralist and $$3\,015$$ sedentary agro-pastoralist households; $$4\,005$$ households are not nomadic pastoralists.
why: **Set out the percentages as decimals.** $$11\% = 0.11$$, $$22\% = 0.22$$ and $$67\% = 0.67$$ of the surveyed households.
**Nomadic pastoralists.** $$0.11 \times 4\,500 = 495$$ households.
**Semi-nomadic pastoralists.** $$0.22 \times 4\,500 = 990$$ households.
**Sedentary agro-pastoralists.** $$0.67 \times 4\,500 = 3\,015$$ households.
**Non-nomadic households and check.** $$4\,500 - 495 = 4\,005$$ households are not nomadic pastoralists; also $$495 + 990 + 3\,015 = 4\,500$$, confirming the allocation.

questions.q: In a district survey, $$670$$ households were classified as sedentary agro-pastoralists and this group made up $$67\%$$ of all the households surveyed. Using the unit's percentages, find the total number of households surveyed and then the number of nomadic and semi-nomadic pastoralist households.
questions.answer: $$1\,000$$ households were surveyed in total: $$110$$ nomadic pastoralist and $$220$$ semi-nomadic pastoralist households.
why: **Work backwards from the known group.** If $$670$$ households are $$67\%$$ of the sample, the total sample $$T$$ satisfies $$0.67 \times T = 670$$.
**Solve for the total.** $$T = \dfrac{670}{0.67} = 1\,000$$ households surveyed.
**Nomadic pastoralist households.** $$0.11 \times 1\,000 = 110$$ households.
**Semi-nomadic pastoralist households.** $$0.22 \times 1\,000 = 220$$ households, and the check $$110 + 220 + 670 = 1\,000$$ confirms the answer.

Using the unit's annual soil-loss estimates of $$50\text{ to }100\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for steep highlands, $$47\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for moist lowlands and $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for dry lowlands, calculate (a) the minimum and (b) the maximum total annual soil loss of the catchment, and (c) the percentage of the minimum total loss that comes from the dry lowland fields.
questions.answer: Minimum total loss = $$27\,100\text{ tons per year}$$; maximum total loss = $$37\,100\text{ tons per year}$$; the dry lowland fields contribute about $$11.1\%$$ of the minimum total loss.
why: **Set up the calculation.** For each zone, soil loss = rate per hectare x area in hectares. Because the steep highland rate is given as a range, the minimum total uses $$50\text{ tons per hectare}$$ and the maximum total uses $$100\text{ tons per hectare}$$.
**Steep highland contribution.** Minimum: $$200 \times 50 = 10\,000\text{ tons}$$; maximum: $$200 \times 100 = 20\,000\text{ tons}$$.
**Moist lowland contribution.** $$300 \times 47 = 14\,100\text{ tons}$$, a single value because only one rate is given.
**Dry lowland contribution.** $$500 \times 6 = 3\,000\text{ tons}$$, also a single value.
**Total the catchment loss.** Minimum total = $$10\,000 + 14\,100 + 3\,000 = 27\,100\text{ tons per year}$$; maximum total = $$20\,000 + 14\,100 + 3\,000 = 37\,100\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Find the dry lowland share of the minimum.** Share = $$\dfrac{3\,000}{27\,100} \times 100\% = 11.07\%$$, which is about $$11.1\%$$.

**Conclude.** The catchment loses between $$27\,100$$ and $$37\,100\text{ tons}$$ of soil each year, and the dry lowland fields - the largest area but the gentlest zone - account for only about $$11.1\%$$ of the minimum total loss.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A catchment in the Asmara highlands has $$400\text{ ha}$$ of steep highland fields, $$250\text{ ha}$$ of moist lowland fields and $$750\text{ ha}$$ of dry lowland fields. Using the unit's rates of $$50\text{ to }100\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for steep highlands, $$47\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for moist lowlands and $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for dry lowlands, find the minimum and maximum total annual soil loss and the percentage of the minimum total that comes from the dry lowland fields.
questions.answer: Minimum total loss = $$36\,250\text{ tons per year}$$; maximum total loss = $$56\,250\text{ tons per year}$$; the dry lowland fields contribute about $$12.4\%$$ of the minimum total loss.
why: **Steep highland contribution.** $$400 \times 50 = 20\,000\text{ tons}$$ at minimum and $$400 \times 100 = 40\,000\text{ tons}$$ at maximum.
**Moist lowland contribution.** $$250 \times 47 = 11\,750\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Dry lowland contribution.** $$750 \times 6 = 4\,500\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Dry lowland share of the minimum.** $$\dfrac{4\,500}{36\,250} \times 100\% = 12.41\%$$, about $$12.4\%$$.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: An extension agent works in a catchment on the Eastern Escarpment that has $$250\text{ ha}$$ of escarpment fields and $$900\text{ ha}$$ of dry lowland fields. The unit's estimates are $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$ per year on the Eastern Escarpment and $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$ per year in the dry lowlands. Calculate the total annual soil loss of the whole catchment and the percentage by which the escarpment fields lose more soil than the dry lowland fields.
questions.answer: Total catchment loss = $$14\,650\text{ tons per year}$$; the escarpment fields lose about $$71.3\%$$ more soil than the dry lowland fields.
why: **Escarpment loss.** $$250\text{ ha} \times 37\text{ tons per hectare} = 9\,250\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Dry lowland loss.** $$900\text{ ha} \times 6\text{ tons per hectare} = 5\,400\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Total catchment loss.** $$9\,250 + 5\,400 = 14\,650\text{ tons per year}$$.
**Percentage excess of the escarpment fields.** Excess = $$9\,250 - 5\,400 = 3\,850\text{ tons}$$; percentage excess = $$\dfrac{3\,850}{5\,400} \times 100\% = 71.3\%$$.
**Conclude.** Although the dry lowland block is more than three times larger in area, its gentler slope means the smaller escarpment block still loses about $$71.3\%$$ more soil than it does.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: The unit shows that agriculture supplies industry with raw materials and also earns Eritrea foreign currency. Choose two products from the unit's agricultural-product table and, for each, trace the chain from farm product to industrial raw material to derived industrial good to non-food by-product. Then explain how the foreign-currency role and the raw-material role reinforce one another in a developing economy such as Eritrea's.
questions.answer: Cotton supplies fiber for clothes, textiles and canvas while its cottonseed cake feeds animals, and malting barley supplies grain starch for beer and malt beverages while brewers' spent grain feeds livestock; exports of farm products such as live animals, skins, hides, meat, oil seeds, cotton and processed fruits and vegetables earn the foreign exchange used to import petroleum, machinery, medicine and fertilizers, and those imports in turn raise the raw-material output that keeps agro-industries and exports growing.
why: **State the chain principle.** Agriculture is the foundation of agro-based industries: each farm product supplies a raw material that industry converts into a main derived good, and the conversion leaves a non-food by-product that is usually returned to agriculture.
**Trace the cotton chain.** Cotton crop -> fiber -> clothes, textiles and canvas, with cottonseed cake left over as an animal feed by-product.
**Trace the malting barley chain.** Malting barley -> grain starch -> beer and malt beverages, with brewers' spent grain left over as a livestock feed by-product.

**Explain the foreign-currency role.** Exporting products such as live animals, skins, hides, meat, oil seeds, cotton and processed fruits and vegetables earns foreign exchange, and that currency is used to import petroleum, machinery, medicine and fertilizers.

**Show how the two roles reinforce each other.** Export earnings pay for the machinery and fertilizer that raise farm output, so more raw material reaches agro-industries and more finished goods and by-products become available; the by-products then lower livestock feed costs, and livestock itself is an export item (live animals, skins, hides), so industrial demand and export earnings continually feed back into farm production.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Sedentary agro-pastoralism (mixed farming) is described in the unit as a highly integrated system. Explain the two-way linkage between crops and livestock in this system and state the approximate share of the Eritrean population that practises it.
questions.answer: Crop residues such as straw are saved to feed the animals during the dry season, and animal manure is returned to the fields to maintain soil fertility; this system represents approximately $$67\%$$ of the population.
why: **Identify the system and its setting.** Sedentary agro-pastoralism is the most dominant farming system in Eritrea, practised in permanent villages of the moist and arid Highlands, where crops and livestock are kept on the same farm.
**Link from crops to livestock.** Crop residues, especially straw, are saved and used as feed for the animals during the dry season, when grazing is scarce.
**Link from livestock back to crops.** Animal manure is returned to the fields to maintain soil fertility, so the livestock enterprise supports the next crop cycle.
**State the population share.** The unit gives this system as approximately $$67\%$$ of the population, compared with $$22\%$$ semi-nomadic and $$11\%$$ nomadic pastoralism.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: The unit states that agriculture has both negative and positive environmental impacts. Using the examples given in the unit, name two negative impacts arising from agricultural chemicals, overgrazing and deforestation, and two positive practices that can be achieved through sustainable management; then explain the unit's pro-tip about balancing economic gains with environmental impacts.
questions.answer: Negative impacts include pollution and damage from the misuse of pesticides, herbicides and synthetic fertilizers, overgrazing, and deforestation; positive impacts come from afforestation, land reclamation, soil conservation and organic manuring, and the pro-tip advises balancing tangible economic gains such as crop yields against intangible environmental effects such as soil erosion or loss of biodiversity so that production remains sustainable.
why: **Recall the negative impacts.** The unit lists the misuse of agricultural chemicals (pesticides, herbicides and synthetic fertilizers), overgrazing, and deforestation as the sources of negative environmental impact.
**Recall the positive practices.** Sustainable practices named in the unit are afforestation, land reclamation, soil conservation and organic manuring.

**Explain the balancing principle.** The pro-tip states that when planning agricultural development you must balance the tangible economic gains, such as crop yields, with the intangible environmental impacts, such as soil erosion or loss of biodiversity.

**State why this matters.** Balancing the two ensures long-term sustainability, because practices that raise yields today but destroy soil and biodiversity reduce the land's productive potential for future seasons.
